title: India Plans First Tokenised Bond Issue in September Using Blockchain Settlement
excerpt: State-owned power financier REC will issue blockchain-settled corporate bonds worth up to $57 million, placing India alongside Europe and Hong Kong in digital securities innovation.
body:
• India will launch its first tokenised corporate bond in September, issued by state-owned power financier REC, worth less than ₹500 crore ($57 million).
  • The bonds will be settled using India's central bank digital currency (CBDC), enabling near-instant settlement through distributed ledger technology.
  • SEBI and the Reserve Bank of India are collaborating on the initiative, which places India alongside Europe and Hong Kong in blockchain-based bond issuance.
  • The pilot will initially be available to a select group of institutional investors and is expected to be unveiled at a Mumbai fintech event.

India's Digital Bond Debut

India is set to issue its first tokenised corporate bonds next month, marking a significant step in the country's adoption of blockchain technology for financial market infrastructure, according to three sources with direct knowledge of the matter who spoke to Reuters.

State-owned power financier REC (formerly Rural Electrification Corporation) will issue the tokenised bonds worth less than 5 billion rupees ($57 million) in what will be a pilot offering available to a select group of institutional investors. The move places India alongside markets such as Europe and Hong Kong that have already adopted blockchain technology for bond issuance and settlement.

Tokenised bonds are securities whose ownership, issuance, trading, and settlement are recorded digitally on a blockchain or distributed ledger, allowing transactions to be completed almost instantly — a sharp contrast to the T+1 or T+2 settlement windows that currently characterize Indian bond markets.

"The offering would be made available to only a select group of investors at the pilot stage."

— Source familiar with the matter, speaking to Reuters

How It Works: CBDC Meets Blockchain

In a notable convergence of India's digital finance initiatives, buyers will use the Reserve Bank of India's central bank digital currency (CBDC) — the digital rupee — to purchase the tokenised bonds, according to one of the sources. This integration effectively creates a fully digital transaction chain, from payment to settlement to ownership recording.

India's markets regulator SEBI and the RBI are working together on pushing the technology, the sources said, speaking on condition of anonymity as discussions are ongoing and confidential. SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey had signaled the initiative at the CareEdge Debt Market Summit in May 2026, where he said the regulator was "exploring a pilot for tokenisation of corporate bonds" that would test whether the technology could deliver "faster settlement, better traceability, automated servicing, and greater transparency."

The offering is expected to be unveiled at an annual financial technology event in Mumbai next month, one of the sources told Reuters. The central bank, markets regulator, and REC did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

Why It Matters for India's Bond Market

India's corporate bond market has long been considered underdeveloped relative to its equity markets. While outstanding corporate bonds have grown, secondary market liquidity remains thin, and settlement processes involve multiple intermediaries and time lags. Tokenisation could address several of these structural challenges.

Distributed ledger technology is already in limited use within India's market infrastructure. National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) and Central Depository Services Limited (CDSL) currently use blockchain-based systems to monitor security creation and covenant compliance in non-convertible securities. The tokenised bond pilot would extend blockchain use from monitoring to the full lifecycle of issuance, trading, and settlement.

"With the RBI having created a digital currency, there is an opportunity to tokenize all financial assets," said Nikhil Aggarwal, founder and group CEO of Grip Invest, a SEBI-regulated investment platform. "This, I believe, is the intention of the regulator."

Global Context and What's Next

India's entry into tokenised bonds follows similar initiatives in other major markets. The European Investment Bank issued a digital bond on Ethereum, while Hong Kong's monetary authority has piloted tokenised green bonds. Singapore's Project Guardian has tested multiple forms of tokenised securities.

While the pilot is modest in size, its implications are significant. If successful, tokenised issuance could lower costs for corporate borrowers, improve price discovery through enhanced transparency, and potentially attract a broader investor base — including retail participants who have largely stayed away from India's bond markets.

SEBI has indicated it will proceed cautiously, noting technological and operational risks. Pandey said the regulator "must move carefully — but we must remain open to useful innovation," adding that quantum computing risks to blockchain security also need to be addressed. A broader rollout could follow six to nine months after the pilot, subject to regulatory comfort and market feedback.
